title: The Missionary Century
subtitle: From Carey's sailing to Edinburgh 1910. How the gospel reached every continent, what it owed and paid to empire, and the local believers who did most of the work.

sections.title: The Map in 1790
sections.body:
Look at the map of the Christian world in 1790 and it is, overwhelmingly, a European map with an American extension. There were old and honorable exceptions. The ancient churches of Ethiopia and Egypt, the Thomas Christians of India, the Orthodox east, and the large Catholic Christendom that Spanish and Portuguese missions had planted across Latin America and the Philippines two centuries earlier, along with hard-won Catholic footholds in China, Vietnam, and Japan, where persecution had nearly erased the church. But Protestantism, born claiming the Bible for everyone, had spent its first two and a half centuries sending almost no one. A few chaplains, the Moravians, scattered efforts among Native Americans. The heirs of the Reformation mostly stayed home and argued.

A century later the picture had changed beyond recognition. By 1910, when a great missionary conference gathered in Edinburgh, there were churches, schools, hospitals, and printing presses on every continent, Scripture in hundreds of languages, and a worldwide web of societies whose reach no church in history had matched. This essay tells how that happened.

It also tells what the change rode in on. The missionary century was also the century of European empire, and the two were tangled at the root, sharing ships, flags, and assumptions. Some missionaries fought the empire's crimes. Some blessed them. Most did both without noticing. The tangle must be told straight, because the people on the receiving end remember it, and because the gospel's escape from that tangle is the best part of the story.

sections.title: Carey and the Use of Means
sections.body:
William Carey made shoes in Northamptonshire, taught himself Greek, Hebrew, and Dutch at the workbench, and pastored a poor Baptist congregation. When he raised the question of missions among the local ministers, tradition has an older man telling him that when God pleased to convert the heathen, he would do it without Carey's help. In 1792 Carey answered with a pamphlet, an enquiry into the obligations of Christians to use means for the conversion of the heathens, whose title carried the whole argument. Waiting on God was disobedience dressed as piety. That spring he preached that the church should expect great things from God and attempt great things for God, as the words have come down to us, and that October, in a widow's back parlor at Kettering, a dozen ministers formed a missionary society and pledged about thirteen pounds.

Carey sailed for India in 1793 and never came home, not once, in forty-one years. The East India Company wanted no missionaries in its territory, so from 1800 the mission settled at the Danish station of Serampore, where Carey, Joshua Marshman, and William Ward formed the steadiest partnership in mission history. They translated. By Carey's death in 1834, the Serampore presses had printed Scripture, whole or in part, in more than forty languages. He also campaigned for decades against sati, the burning of widows, and lived to see it outlawed in 1829.

His first years were brutal. Poverty, malaria, a dead child, a wife broken by grief and mental illness, and seven years before the first Indian convert. He stayed. The century that followed walked through the door that stubbornness opened.

sections.title: Societies, Judsons, Taylor, Livingstone
sections.body:
What Kettering started, the English-speaking world copied within a generation. The London Missionary Society came in 1795, the Church Missionary Society in 1799, the British and Foreign Bible Society in 1804, the American Board in 1810. In 1812 Adoniram and Ann Judson sailed for Asia and ended in Burma, where Adoniram survived a year and a half in a death prison during the Anglo-Burmese war and finished the Burmese Bible in 1834. Ann had died in 1826, one of the first of thousands of missionary wives and single women whose graves mark the century. By its end, women outnumbered men on many fields, running schools and clinics a century before their home churches would let them preach.

Hudson Taylor broke the next barrier. China's treaty ports had missionaries, but the vast interior had none, so in 1865 Taylor, praying on Brighton beach, founded the China Inland Mission with ten pounds and a request to God for twenty-four workers. His people wore Chinese dress, moved far up-country, and were promised no salary, only prayer. At his death in 1905 the mission numbered more than eight hundred missionaries.

And David Livingstone, missionary turned explorer, crossed Africa preaching Christianity, commerce, and civilization as one package, a formula whose second and third terms would cost the first one dearly. When he died in 1873, his companions Chuma and Susi buried his heart under a tree and carried his body a thousand miles to the coast so that Westminster Abbey could have the rest. The gesture said more about Africa's place in this story than England yet understood.

sections.title: The Gospel and the Gunboat
sections.body:
Now the tangle, told straight. The missionary century moved on imperial rails. In India the empire first barred missionaries and then, from 1813, licensed them. The treaties that ended the Opium Wars, in 1842 and 1858, forced China open to Western trade and wrote toleration of Christian missions into the settlement, so that the faith arrived in company with a drug most missionaries despised. Many of them shared the era's racial contempt, treated European customs as Christian requirements, and read the empire's advance as providence. The association had a price, and Chinese Christians paid the worst of it in 1900, when the Boxer Rising killed thousands of native believers, and scores of missionary families with them, as agents of foreign power.

But the ledger has a second column. Missionary agitation helped force the abolition of slavery across the British Empire, with men like William Knibb of Jamaica campaigning in Britain until emancipation came. Missionary witnesses, cameras in hand, helped expose the atrocities of the Congo Free State, and an African American minister, George Washington Williams, named those crimes in an open letter to the Belgian king in 1890.

And the deepest subversion was the missionaries' own method. They translated. Putting Scripture into a people's mother tongue told that people, against every colonial assumption, that God spoke their language and had no favorite race. Converts read Exodus and drew conclusions. The empires shipped a book that condemned them, and the shipping clerks rarely noticed. The scholar Lamin Sanneh spent a career showing what that translation set loose.

sections.title: Crowther and the Local Evangelists
sections.body:
The word missionary calls up a white face, and that is the century's most durable distortion. Most of the actual evangelizing was done by local believers whose names the sending churches never learned. African catechists walked the bush paths. Chinese Bible women, as the missions called them, went house to house where no foreigner could enter. Pacific islander teachers carried the faith from island to island and died on beaches no European had mapped. When the histories were written in London and New York, these workers became scenery. They were the engine.

One name can stand for the multitude, because his story carries both the glory and the shame. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Yoruba boy, was seized by slave raiders in 1821, freed at sea by a British anti-slavery patrol, and educated in Sierra Leone, where he was baptized. He became a scholar, led the translation of the Yoruba Bible, and in 1864 was consecrated the first African Anglican bishop. For a generation he oversaw the Niger mission. Then the climate hardened. A race-proud younger generation of Englishmen arrived in the 1880s, dismantled his work around him, and humiliated the old man until he died in 1891. His successor was white. The lesson Europe taught, that Africans could be converts but never leaders, took most of a century to unlearn, and the independent churches that later swept the continent were, in part, the bill for it.

Add the martyrs of Uganda, dozens of young converts burned for the faith in the 1880s, whose deaths seeded one of the fastest growing churches on earth, and Pandita Ramabai in India, scholar and rescuer of widows and famine orphans, translating Scripture into Marathi. The century belongs to them as much as to Carey.

sections.title: Edinburgh 1910 and the Verdict
sections.body:
In June of 1910, more than twelve hundred delegates gathered in Edinburgh for the World Missionary Conference, the summit of the Protestant century. Its chairman, the American layman John Mott, had helped build a student movement on the watchword that the world could be evangelized in that generation, and the mood in the hall was confidence. The maps were surveyed, the statistics compiled, the strategies drawn. Christianity stood on every continent, and the men in that room, nearly all of them Western, believed the work was nearly theirs to finish.

The composition of the hall told the deeper truth. Of those twelve hundred delegates, fewer than twenty came from the younger churches of Asia, and from Africa almost none. One of the few, V. S. Azariah of India, soon to be a bishop, thanked the missionaries for their sacrifices and then asked them for the one thing they had rarely given. Not money, not workers. Friends. The room heard it as the rebuke it was, and the century that followed proved his point. Within sixty years the empires that had carried the missionaries were gone. The churches they left behind not only survived the empires' fall. They outgrew the churches that had sent to them.

So the verdict on the missionary century must hold two truths the way the century itself never could. The gospel really did go to the whole world, at staggering personal cost, sped by an empire it did not create and could not control. And the peoples who received it sorted the treasure from the packaging better than the senders did. God, it turns out, had used the ships without blessing the cargo manifests. He had done it before, with Roman roads. The pattern is the point.

keyFigures.name: William Carey
keyFigures.note: Shoemaker, translator, and founder of the modern Protestant missionary movement.

keyFigures.name: Ann and Adoniram Judson
keyFigures.note: American pioneers in Burma. He translated the Burmese Bible. She kept him alive in prison to finish it.

keyFigures.name: Hudson Taylor
keyFigures.note: Founder of the China Inland Mission, who took the gospel up-country in Chinese dress.

keyFigures.name: David Livingstone
keyFigures.note: Missionary explorer whose formula of Christianity and commerce carried both blessing and bill.

keyFigures.name: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
keyFigures.note: Freed slave, Yoruba translator, and the first African Anglican bishop, shamefully sidelined at the end.

keyFigures.name: Pandita Ramabai
keyFigures.note: Indian scholar and reformer who served widows and orphans and translated Scripture into Marathi.
